summary.text: A 54-year-old man living in a nursing home, with prior strokes (old right frontal parietal and more recent left frontal and parietal ACA-distribution infarction) and residual right hemiparesis, CKD stage IIIb, type II diabetes with retinopathy, congestive heart failure, hyperlipidemia, left retinal detachment with left-eye blindness, depression, obstructive sleep apnea and hypertension, presented for confusion compared with his orientation baseline. He denied pain, dyspnea, chills, cold sweats and fever; examination showed right-sided weakness with 5/5 strength and was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory workup included creatinine 5.2 mg/dL, eGFR 12, BUN 83 mg/dL, sodium 143, chloride 112, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, venous pCO2 44.6 mmHg, bicarbonate 15.4 mEq/L and pH 7.16, a CBC reported as within normal limits, and CT head without contrast showing no acute changes. MRI brain showed chronic ischemic changes without acute abnormality.

On the seventh day of admission he developed continuous regular small jerky movements of the right upper extremity every two to three seconds, lasting six to eight hours per episode, with preserved consciousness and awareness and no tongue biting, sphincter loss or generalized tonic-clonic movement. Ativan 2 mg IV partially improved the symptoms before recurrence after an hour. Continuous EEG over three interpretations showed left-predominant slowing and no seizures or epileptiform discharges, with right-hand twitching on video and no clear ictal EEG pattern.

DDS-induced seizure was initially considered but judged less likely, and the clinical and laboratory workup was negative for toxic-metabolic etiologies, infection or sepsis. EPC was suspected and clinically diagnosed. He was started on IV levetiracetam 1.5 g loading, then PO 500 mg BID with an additional 250 mg after dialysis, plus lacosamide 100 mg BID, with planned frequent AED level monitoring, and tolerated them without reported side effects.

The jerky movements progressively shortened; two days before discharge episodes lasted no longer than one hour and were milder, and on the last day before discharge he was symptom-free. He was discharged with nephrology and neurology outpatient follow-up.
